pages.title: Of the Pontiff, Who Is an Office
pages.by: [DRAFT] Copied from the Warden's board at Nine Stairs, where the teaching stands to be read aloud and not copied.
pages.bb:
[DRAFT] Teaching given to the talliers of the fourth wall on the night before they are first let onto the Fifth Stair, in the chapter-house of the Kostyak. To be read aloud by the Warden or his voice. Not to be copied.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]What the Pontiff is[/color][/font_size]

You have counted bones for six years and you have not yet counted a brother. Tonight you learn the one count the Order keeps that is not a count of bones. Attend.

The Marrow Pontiff is not a brother. He is not a bone. He is an office, as Sweeper is an office and Tallier is an office and Warden is an office, and like those it is filled, and emptied, and filled. The lowland priests gave us the word Pontiff, which in their mouths means a maker of bridges, and we let them keep it, because they are not wrong and because the true word is not for the lowlands. On the stairs we say the Kneeling.

Here is why. The Mother bears the Hide. She has borne it since she fell, and she has never once set it down, and one who bears cannot kneel. Try it with a sack of grit across your shoulders; you will not get your knee to the floor without the sack coming off. So the Order kneels for her. One brother, in one place, always. That brother is the Pontiff. The office is to kneel in the marrow until the count closes.

That is all the office is. Whatever else you have heard, from salt-carriers or sweepers or the long ones on the lowest stair, is not the teaching. The teaching is a knee on a floor.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]Of the well[/color][/font_size]

The wells are many at the lip and one at the bottom. You have drawn chrism from the Second and the Seventh and you have never been let near the Fifth, which is capped, and the cap sealed, and no brother draws there. The Fifth is the lip the Pontiff went down by. It is not the only lip he can be reached at. Three days past the thighbone citadel there is a slab laid across four knuckles with OLD UPRIGHT cut in its face, and behind it a lip of polished stone with a stair cut down the inside wall, and the steps of that stair are too deep for a man's leg, because they were cut for one going down to kneel and not for one coming up.

A pilgrim at the knuckles and a Warden at the Fifth cap hear the same slow voice. Novices take this for a marvel. It is not. It is one office speaking, and an office has as many mouths as it has doors.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]Of what the office does[/color][/font_size]

It counts. Whoever comes to a lip is counted, crown to sole, each number laid on its bone like a thumb. Then the office says one of two words: open, or closed. Two hundred and six is eight, and eight is open, and most who come to the lip go away open and in good health, and die open, and are laid open, and the Mother bears them so.

To one who kneels, the office may give the Mother's gift. You know the gift as a figure in a niche-tally that stands higher than the dead brought in. At the lip it is one bone, given to the frame of one who knelt, so that two hundred and six becomes two hundred and seven, and eight becomes nine, and a count is closed in the living, which the Rule allows nowhere else. The gift is not asked for. It is not refused. Do not go to the lip looking for it.

This is why the Pontiff is the Mother's herald and no other thing is. She has no mouth. The Hush has no mouth for numbers. Between them kneels an office that speaks in numbers only, and so says nothing the Hush can unsay.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]Of the succession[/color][/font_size]

When the Pontiff's own count closes, the office is empty, and the Order fills it. The Chapter chooses an Ossuarch whose frame is closed and whose number is read aloud nine times without a brother objecting. He lays his name in a niche, if he has not already. He goes down to the Fifth, and the cap is lifted, and the seal is cut, and he goes down the stair cut inside the wall, on his hands, as the Order climbs every old stair, and he does not come up. The cap is set back and sealed before the chrism is cold.

Of the laying of the one before him the Order teaches this, and only this: the Mother lays him herself. She lays nothing else. No brother has seen it. No brother asks.

The roll of the Kneeling is kept on the Fifth Stair in chrism ink, numbers only, and it is read at the Feast of the Laying after the Count and before the dust goes up. It stands at eleven. The eleven are: nine; eighteen; one hundred and eight; one thousand and seventeen; two thousand one hundred and six; three thousand and fifteen; four thousand one hundred and thirty-one; five thousand and four; six thousand and twelve; seven thousand and two; eight thousand and one. Each closes to nine, as a Pontiff's number must. The one who kneels now is not read until he is laid.

Eleven is two. The Order knows it. An office is an open count by its nature, for it is not finished until it is finished with, and the Rule has nothing to say about the root of an office. Do not raise it with your Warden.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]Of the heresy of the one bone[/color][/font_size]

Now the thing you were brought here to be told, so that when you hear it on the stair you will know it for what it is.

There are brothers, sweepers mostly, and some who have been too long on the lowest stair with the long ones, who say that there has only ever been one. They say he went down before the stair was cut, and knelt, and has knelt since, and has never been replaced, because nothing has ever been found to replace him with. They say the eleven on the roll are one bone written eleven times in eleven inks. They say that each Ossuarch sent down the Fifth did not fill the office but was added to it, joint upon joint, hand upon hand, and that this is why those who have seen the top of him rise at a lip count fingers past thirty and lose their place. They say the lower letters on the slab at the knuckles, the ones worn to a shine under OLD UPRIGHT, are not letters, and are one notch.

Hear the Order's answer, and give it in these words when you are asked.

A count that never closes is an open count. The Mother keeps no open count. Therefore there is not one Pontiff; there is a succession, and each closed, and each was laid.

As to the fingers: when a Pontiff is laid his hands are laid as he knelt, pressed tip to tip, and the hands of the next are set upon them, as a brother sets a skull upon the skulls before it in a niche that is full. That is the office showing. It is not a man.

As to the notch: the Order did not cut the slab at the knuckles, and does not read what it did not cut.

Whoever says there is one shall be set to the stair, and shall count the stair until he comes to a different figure, and shall be written in the book as carrying an open count, and shall carry it behind his teeth until it closes. He is not to be struck. The Rule does not strike for arithmetic.

Ask nothing of the Ninth Stair. Ask less of the Fifth. Go down to your wall.

[indent][i][color=#c8bfae]In the lower margin, in a sweeper's small hand and a different ink: Eleven is two. Two is open. Count again, Warden. I did, on the stair, and I came to one.[/color][/i][/indent]

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— Read by the Tallier of the Fourth Wall, who is written Three Thousand Two Hundred and Four.[/color][/i][/right]

pages.title: Instruction for the Sister Who Takes the Cup
pages.by: [DRAFT] Written for a sister of Sallow Lip on the back leaves of a tithe-roll by the eldest there, and not burned.
pages.bb:
[DRAFT] You have been given a cup. It is not yours; it is the house's, and before it was the house's it was hers. Read this once before the Day of the Measure and once with the cup in your hands, and then burn it, for the Rule allows one book in a house and this is not it.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]Of the cup[/color][/font_size]

The tithe-cup is thrown from the red clay of the lower lip and fired in the gutter-kiln, and it holds one measure to the ring and no more. If yours holds more, it is not a tithe-cup; bring it to me. Hold it in the left hand. The right arm is for opening.

She takes a measure. She does not take a flood. The flood is what the fattening houses give her, by the bucket, out of captives, and they call it feasting, and she takes it as the gutter takes rain, without knowing whose it was. A measure she knows. That is the whole difference between us and the Laden Board, and it is the whole of our Rule, and you will hear it said more plainly than this: blood given is a word said to someone.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]Of the measure[/color][/font_size]

A word must be whole to be heard. So the measure is whole. Fill to the ring and stop. The sister who overfills has said too much, and the too-much runs over the lip of the cup into the dust and is nobody's. The sister who underfills has said nothing, and will stand at the wound all night with a cup in her hand like a woman who has forgotten what she came to say.

In the mother-house the sangrador opens, and the one who opens never opens himself. We have no sangrador at Sallow Lip and have not had one in forty years. You will open yourself. The horn knife, inside the elbow, never the wrist. The wrist is a flood.

Count while it runs. The count is not a prayer. It is so that you know when to stop.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]Of the words[/color][/font_size]

She has three names and they are said in the old order and no other.

The Maiden first, for she is the wound that gives, and it is to the wound you are speaking. The Mother second, for she is the wheel that turns what is given back into flesh, and without the second name the first is a word with no answer. The Nurse third, and once, and never twice, and never alone.

You will ask why the third is said at all, if I am going to warn you against her, and I am. The third is said because a word must come to its end, and the end of her is the Nurse, as the end of a meal is the one who clears it. You say it to close the mouth of the cup. You say it once.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]Of the lip[/color][/font_size]

Set the cup on the lip of the wound at dusk, upright, at your own place, and go in. Do not watch it.

At dawn, go and look. If the cup is empty and dry, she has drunk, and you have been heard. If it is empty and wet, something else drank, and you will tell me, and we will count the pegs together. If it is standing full, with the blood in it gone dark, then it was not taken; I have known that happen to a house once, and the house is bare pegs now and a wound that drinks alone, and you will not ask me more about Villa Llaga.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]Of what comes to the lip[/color][/font_size]

Below the lower lip, where the wound narrows and the ground is soft, there is a slab with letters on it: THE RED MOTHER. The house does not pray there, and you will not. We keep the slab swept and we leave it alone. It is the Nurse's. She wakes at it.

She comes to the one who has bled too much. The sister who overfilled. The brother whose welts will not close. The woman on the moor whose child is lying wrong. She comes in whether the door is barred or not, and a line of wet comes in behind her across the floor. She is taller than the door and does not stoop for it. Her front is soaked dark from the throat down. She smells of copper and of warm bread. She kneels, and the floor gives under her knee as ash gives, and when she has knelt she is still above you.

She is kind. Hear me, sister, for this is the thing you will not believe until you see it, and then you will believe nothing else: she is kind. She will say she has room.

[font_size=26][color=#c9974a]Of the Nurse, and what she asks[/color][/font_size]

She asks to take it. The bleeding. The scourge. The cup. She asks for nothing you were ever taught to refuse. She asks to help. She will offer with her hands open and her eyes on yours and she will mean it, and the bleeding will stop as if a hand had been laid flat on it, and you will sleep.

Refuse her.

If you let her take the bleeding, you will never bleed again. Cut yourself the next morning and the edges will close before a drop comes. You will stand at the lip on the Day of the Measure with a dry cup in your left hand and a dry knife in your right, and you will not be punished, for there is nothing in the Rule about it; you will only not be heard. A sister who cannot give is not cast out. She is outside already. She has no word to say.

That is the first of what she asks, and it is not the worst. The worst is that she keeps what she nurses. She will know your name, the one your mother said once into your hair before anyone else had heard it, and she will say it to you as she takes the bleeding, kindly, and you will hear that it is already worn smooth, as a word is worn smooth by a mouth that has been saying it a long time. Then you are hers, as the fed are the feeder's. When you are laid out at last, the Pale will come for your frame and the Brotherhood will come for your meat, and both will find there is nothing to part, because both were given away already, in one night, to someone who asked nicely.

I have known one who let her. She is alive and warm and does not bleed, and nobody in this house can hold her name in the mouth longer than a breath; it goes back to the Nurse the way water goes back to the low place.

The Maiden gives. The Nurse takes, and gives back only milk. Give to the Maiden.

Burn this. Fill the cup to the ring. Say the third name once.

[right][i][color=#c9974a]— The eldest of Sallow Lip, who has given forty-one measures and has one more in her, and will say the third name once.[/color][/i][/right]
